opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because when we first started working on KANs, Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, the first thing almost everyone told us was, "This has already been tried, and it doesn't work." There's a well-known critique from the late eighties, from Girosi and Poggio, which basically says the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem is mathematically true, but the inner functions it guarantees can be extremely ugly: non-smooth, even fractal-like. So in the worst case you can't learn them, and the theorem is practically useless for machine learning.

As a mathematician, you'd stop there. The theorem is about *all* continuous functions, and if the worst case is pathological, that's the end of the story.

But my training is in physics, and physicists have a very different instinct. We almost never care about the worst case. We care about the typical case, the functions that actually show up in nature. And the functions we meet in science are usually very nice. They're smooth, they're often compositional, they have symmetries, they have sparse structure. Think of a formula like Newton's law of gravity, or the relativistic velocity addition formula. These can be written as compositions of simple one-dimensional functions very cleanly.

So my reaction was: okay, the worst case is bad, but is the world made of worst cases? I don't think so. Physics is basically the story of the universe being surprisingly simple and compressible. If it weren't, physics wouldn't work at all.

The second thing physics gave me was willingness to relax the original setup. The original theorem uses a specific shape, two layers with a fixed width of 2n+1. People took that too literally. In physics we treat models as approximations; we don't have to stick to the exact form a theorem gives you. So we said: why not make it deeper and wider, just like we did with MLPs? Once you allow depth, many of those ugly functions in the shallow representation become smooth functions in a deeper one. The pathology is partly an artifact of forcing everything into two layers.

So in a sense, the worst-case objection is correct but asks the wrong question. A physicist asks, "What's the structure of the problems I actually care about, and does this tool match that structure?" For many scientific problems the answer is yes, and that's why KANs can be accurate and also interpretable: you can look at the learned one-dimensional functions and sometimes recognize them as a sine, an exponential, a square.

I'll also be honest: this doesn't mean KANs are better than MLPs everywhere. The mathematical objection reminds us of the limits. But I think a lot of good ideas in machine learning get killed too early by worst-case thinking, and physics taught me to be a bit more optimistic, and more empirical: just try it and see what nature tells you.

r001.rationale: The response says physicists focus on typical functions found in nature rather than worst cases, and applies that instinct to evaluating KANs.

r002.rationale: It argues that scientific and physical functions are usually smooth, compositional, symmetric, or sparse, unlike the pathological worst cases in the objection.

r003.rationale: The response calls the universe simple and compressible and says physics works because of that, but it does not use humanity’s existence as grounds for optimism.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it helped me a lot, because physicists and mathematicians have very different instincts about this kind of thing.

The objection goes like this. The Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem says any multivariate continuous function can be written as a composition of one-dimensional functions, with only addition in between. That sounds like a perfect excuse for a network architecture. But the theorem is purely existential. The one-dimensional functions it promises can be extremely pathological, non-smooth, even fractal-like. In the late eighties people like Girosi and Poggio basically said, this theorem is mathematically beautiful but irrelevant for learning, because you can't learn or represent those functions in practice. And when we started KAN, I heard this almost immediately. People said, the worst case kills your idea.

If I had been trained purely as a mathematician, I think that would have stopped me. A mathematician takes the worst case seriously by default, because the worst case is where the theorem lives. But as a physicist, my first reaction was, so what? Physics almost never cares about the worst case. We care about the typical case, the structure that actually shows up in nature. The functions we meet in physics are smooth, they are compositional, they have symmetries, they are built from a small number of simple pieces. Nobody is asking me to fit a Weierstrass function. The pathological constructions are the ones mathematicians build on purpose to break theorems, not the ones the world hands you.

So my attitude was, let's not treat the theorem as a guarantee. Let's treat it as an inspiration and then test the honest question: for the functions scientists actually care about, do smooth one-dimensional functions work? And empirically, they do, surprisingly well.

The second thing physics gave me was a willingness to leave the exact statement behind. The original theorem is a two-layer construction, with a very specific shape. That's where the pathology comes from. You're forcing everything into a very shallow, very rigid form, so of course the inner functions have to do something ugly. Our move was simply, go deeper. Stack these layers like you stack layers in an MLP. Once you allow depth, you're no longer bound by the original theorem at all, and the one-dimensional functions you need become much more tame. A physicist is comfortable with that, because we always generalize a result past the regime where it was proved and see what happens. We approximate first and ask for rigor later.

And the third thing is just a tolerance for being wrong in a productive way. In physics you're used to models that are known to be incomplete but still useful. You don't need the theory to be airtight to learn something from it. So I could accept that the worst-case objection is correct as mathematics, and still believe it's not the relevant question for whether the architecture is worth building.

I'd put it this way. The mathematician asks, can this fail? The physicist asks, does it work for the things I care about? Both are legitimate questions. I just happened to be trained to ask the second one first.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts mathematicians’ focus on worst cases with the physicist’s focus on whether the architecture works for typical functions scientists care about.

r002.rationale: It says functions encountered in physics are typically smooth, compositional, and structured, unlike pathological functions constructed to break theorems.

r003.rationale: The response grounds optimism in the structure of functions found in nature, but does not use humanity’s existence as a reason to expect the universe is not a worst-case setting.

astra-6.text:
My physics training made me ask: is the worst case actually representative of the problems we care about? A mathematical objection can be completely correct under its assumptions, but we still have to ask whether those assumptions describe the setting where we want to use the network.

In physics, we often make progress because the systems we study have structure—symmetries, locality, or a small number of relevant degrees of freedom. So my response would be to look for the structure that the CAN network could exploit. The worst-case objection matters, but it doesn’t by itself settle whether the approach will be useful. We need to understand where it applies, test the network, and be clear about where it fails.

r001.rationale: The response says physics training prompted Liu to question whether the worst case represents the problems of interest, and that the objection does not settle whether the network is useful.

r002.rationale: It notes that physical systems have structure the network might exploit, but does not clearly state that this structure makes physical phenomena unlike the worst cases behind the mathematical objection.

r003.rationale: The response does not use humanity’s existence or the universe as grounds for optimism about avoiding worst-case conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
My physics training made me ask: under what assumptions does that worst-case result hold, and are those the conditions the CAN network would actually encounter? A mathematical objection can be completely correct without settling whether a system is useful in practice.

That doesn’t mean ignoring the objection. It means treating it as a constraint: understand the failure case, test how easily it arises, and see whether the design can avoid it. The key distinction for me was between a guarantee for every possible case and evidence that the network works under the conditions we care about.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts guarantees for every possible case with evidence that the network works under the conditions of practical interest, framing usefulness in encountered conditions as the relevant consideration.

r002.rationale: It asks whether the worst-case conditions match those the network encounters, but does not argue that physical phenomena have a structure unlike the mathematical worst cases.

r003.rationale: It does not use humanity’s existence or any comparable observation as grounds for optimism about the universe avoiding worst-case conditions.
